title: Experimental Evidence on Negative Impact of Generative AI on Scientific Learning Outcomes (A Pilot Research)
extended_summary:
This pilot study investigates whether generative AI helps or harms learning effectiveness when people read academic materials and complete related writing tasks. The paper is motivated by growing interest in using tools such as ChatGPT in education, alongside concern that AI may improve writing productivity while weakening actual comprehension and learning. The study is not about K-12 foundational reading; instead, it examines scientific/academic reading comprehension among highly educated adults.

The intervention compared three experimentally assigned task conditions across three reading-writing cycles: (1) manual summary writing without AI, (2) AI-supported summary writing, and (3) an "Active" AI-assisted reading/chat condition in which participants could use AI to ask questions to support comprehension rather than write a summary. Participants read adapted college/postgraduate-level passages, completed writing tasks under time limits, and then answered five multiple-choice comprehension questions after each passage. Writing quality and time-on-task were also recorded.

The sample consisted of 32 college-educated participants recruited online through Prolific. The paper describes them as college-educated individuals from a range of academic backgrounds; many appear to hold advanced degrees, and the materials were explicitly at college/postgraduate difficulty. The study occurred online over a short period in August 2023, with no classroom or school-supported implementation and no teacher involvement.

The main conclusion is that generative AI use reduced immediate comprehension accuracy relative to manual work in this setting. The author reports average correctness of 66.7% in the manual condition versus 48.4% in the AI-writing condition and 48.9% in the AI-assisted active reading condition, with regression-adjusted declines of 25.1% and 12%, respectively. At the same time, AI improved writing quality and speed. The paper argues that overreliance on generative AI may undermine learning even when it boosts productivity, and that benefits may depend on prior knowledge and language proficiency. For the user's retrieval topic, this is only adjacent evidence: it is not a K-12 study, not about foundational reading outcomes, and not direct causal evidence for classroom reading instruction.
quality_tier_rationale: Although the paper uses an experimental design, it is a small pilot preprint with n=32, conducted on college-educated Prolific adults rather than K-12 learners in classrooms or school-supported settings. It is therefore not credible direct evidence for the retrieved K-12 foundational reading question and falls well outside the target population and context.
impact_tier_rationale: The direct learning outcome most relevant here is negative: AI and AI-assisted conditions reduced reading-comprehension accuracy relative to manual work. Any productivity or writing-quality gains do not offset the negative academic learning result for the target causal-outcome lens.

interventions.use_case: Participants used ChatGPT/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 either to generate summary writing for academic reading passages or to engage in guided chat/active reading to help understand college-level texts before answering comprehension questions.
Generative AI was used as a writing assistant to produce or help produce summaries of assigned readings, with writing quality and completion time compared against manual writing.

finding.finding_summary: In this pilot randomized experimental task study, 32 college-educated participants completed manual, AI-writing, and AI-assisted active reading conditions around college/postgraduate-level reading passages. Relative to manual writing (mean accuracy 66.7%), full AI reliance reduced comprehension-question accuracy to 48.4%, and AI-assisted active reading yielded 48.9%; regression-adjusted estimates reported a 25.1% drop for full AI reliance and a 12% drop for partial AI reliance, both statistically significant. This is direct generative-AI evidence on reading comprehension, but it is not K-12, not foundational reading, and uses adult academic reading materials rather than classroom ELA instruction.
finding.measure: Accuracy on five multiple-choice comprehension questions after each reading/writing cycle
finding.effect_size: 25.1% reduction (AI vs manual, adjusted); 12% reduction (AI-assisted active reading vs manual, adjusted)
finding.std_deviation: Manual SD=0.266287; AI SD=0.287588; Active SD=0.3178209

finding.finding_summary: Generative AI improved task efficiency in the writing component: participants in AI and Active conditions finished earlier on average than those in the manual condition. The paper reports average completion times of 8.7 minutes for AI and 9 minutes for Active, while nearly all manual participants used the full allotted time, indicating faster production with AI support, though no inferential effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Task completion time/productivity during summary-writing or AI-assisted reading tasks

finding.finding_summary: For the writing product itself, AI-generated/assisted summaries were rated higher than manual writing on flow, grammar, and coverage using 1-5 scoring rubrics. The study describes improved writing quality under AI assistance but does not report exact mean differences, standardized effect sizes, or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: Summary-writing quality ratings on comprehensiveness/coverage, grammar, and flow (1-5 scales)
